narrative: Star Vetter automatically finds candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite and vets them using a rigorous pipeline. We start with light curves from over 10,000 stars, apply statistical checks to catch real signals, cross-match against six major variable-star catalogs to flag known objects, and then run an automated pixel-level check to confirm that the signal comes from the target star and not a nearby contaminant. So far we have confirmed 160 candidates. To improve our vetting, we trained a machine-learning model on 1,572 labeled examples that outperforms our baseline approach, giving us a second opinion on candidate quality. The results are trustworthy because they survive multiple independent filters: statistical rigor, novelty screening, automated image checks, and comparison with established catalogs. Every candidate listed here has passed all of these gates.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars that orbit each other in a plane aligned with Earth. As they orbit, each star periodically passes in front of the other from our viewpoint, blocking some of its light. This creates a regular dip in brightness that we can see in TESS data. By measuring how deep and frequent these dips are, we can learn about the stars' sizes, brightness, and orbital periods.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' candidate on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is any star that passes our statistical vetting and novelty checks. A confirmed candidate is one that has also passed our automated pixel-level check - meaning the signal genuinely comes from the target star itself and is not contamination from a nearby star. Only confirmed candidates appear in the main listing on this site.

faqs.question: What is the machine-learning score, and what does it do?
faqs.answer: We trained a machine-learning model on 1,572 hand-labeled examples to provide a second opinion on candidate quality. It outperforms our rule-based baseline approach. The score is informational only - it does not currently gate which candidates get checked or how they are processed. It is one way to assess confidence in a result.

faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check if a candidate is real?
faqs.answer: After statistical and novelty vetting, every candidate goes through an automated pixel-level check. This algorithm examines the image data to confirm that the signal comes from the target star and not from a nearby contaminant star. The check is fully automated and runs on every candidate that reaches that stage of the pipeline.

faqs.question: What if the orbital period looks like it might be aliased?
faqs.answer: We run an odd/even eclipse-depth test: we compare the brightness dips from odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered ones. If they differ significantly, it suggests the period we measured might be an alias - a harmonic or sub-harmonic of the true period. When this test flags a candidate, we note it on the candidate's page so you are aware of the caveat.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. TESS data is public, and the light curves we analyze are available through the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST). You can download the data, search for the target by its TIC ID, and inspect the light curve yourself to see the eclipses and judge the result.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on Star Vetter?
faqs.answer: Being listed on this site is where the Star Vetter pipeline itself ends. The candidate is no longer processed by this automated system. What happens next - whether it receives follow-up observations, spectroscopic analysis, or inclusion in a catalog - is outside the scope of this project. The site provides the data and vetting; future steps are up to the broader astronomical community.
